html.hero.lead: A hand-made Neapolitan pizza dough recipe over three days, calibrated by the first bake. Adjust the parameters; quantities, schedule and instructions recalculate. The dough matters more than the clock.
html.panel.title: Parameters
html.panel.note: Defaults = version 1.0, consolidated after the first bake. Your values are saved in this browser.
html.recipe.sub: Total quantities and how they split between preferment and final dough.
html.sched.sub: Tell it when you want to bake. The plan is worked out backwards; treat the times as a guide.
html.steps.sub: Tick each step when done. Tags show the source: base recipe, adaptation for home baking, or a lesson from the first bake.
html.oven.sub: Bench timer and diagnosis by result. The first pizza of each session calibrates the oven.

html.rules.sub: The bottleneck right now isn't the dough. It's heat calibration and the technique for stretching and topping.

rules: Don't raise the hydration yet.
Don't swap out the Caputo Pizzeria flour.
Don't over-knead. Use rest and folds.
Salt before oil.
Use bassinage for the last of the water.
Oil always goes in last.
Sticky dough during mixing gets no extra flour.
Don't re-ball the dough before stretching.
Don't use a rolling pin.
Don't press the cornicione.
Knock excess flour off the base.
Light on sauce, light on cheese.
A topped pizza doesn't wait on the peel.
Check that it slides before launching.
Control top and stone separately.
The first pizza calibrates the session.
Let the stone recover between pizzas.
Watch the dough more than the clock.
Change one relevant variable at a time.
Next session: less heat underneath, same recipe.
glossary: Holding back part of the water and working it in gradually once the gluten has started to form.
Each individual dough ball. It becomes one pizza. Plural: panetti.
The raised, airy rim. Preserved by pushing the gas from the centre outwards.
Stretching the dough into a rectangle on the bench and folding it. No rolling pin.
Small dark spots spread across the cornicione. Not the same as charred patches.
Flour, the same weight of water and all the yeast. 100% hydration, close to a poolish.

Turn according to colour. Watch the cornicione.

li: Dry-mix {pfFlour} g of flour with {yeast} g of yeast.
Add {pfWater} g of water and stir into a rough paste with no dry flour left.
Cover. Leave 1 h at room temperature.
Refrigerate ({fridge} °C) for about {pfh} h.
items.tip: The original recipe calls for 12–16 h at 12 °C. In a colder fridge, the longer time makes up for it. Ready when it's bubbly, has internal structure and shows no sign of collapse.

li: Use the preferment straight from the fridge, without a long warm-up.
Add {finFlour} g of flour and {initWater} g of water.
Mix until all the flour is hydrated. It doesn't need to be smooth.
Cover and rest. Time develops the gluten for you.
Dissolve {salt} g of salt in {saltWater} g of water.
Add the solution little by little, using pincer movements and folds.
Wait for each portion to be absorbed before the next.
items.tip: Salt always goes in before the oil.

li: Add the remaining {bassWater} g of water in small portions.
Only add more once the dough has absorbed the previous one.
If the dough gets sticky, don't add flour.
Alternate rests and sets of folds, without aggressive kneading.
Stop when the dough is smooth, rounded, elastic and has surface tension.
items.tip: On the first bake, time and rest did most of the work. Don't chase a perfectly smooth dough with non-stop kneading.

li: With the dough already structured, add {oil} g of olive oil a little at a time.
Work it in with pincers and folds until fully absorbed.
items.tip: The dough turns slippery and shiny and seems weaker. That's normal. Don't add flour.

li: Rest 3–5 min.
Lamination: gently stretch the dough into a rectangle on the bench and fold it over itself. No rolling pin, no tearing.
Shape into a ball. Rest 15 min.
Do gentle folds and rest for about 1 h.
Divide into {n} dough balls of {per} g (total dough {total} g).
Ball with surface tension and seal the base well.
Covered container, in the fridge for about {panh} h.
items.tip: Base recipe: 24–36 h at 5 °C. At {fridge} °C fermentation moves faster; judge by appearance.

li: Take them out of the fridge about {outh} h before baking (reference: ~26 °C).
Ready when: risen, lots of small bubbles and a few bigger ones, airy sides, holds its shape, no collapse, relaxed.
In a 1 L tub, the reference is the dough reaching halfway.
items.tip: warn|Don't re-ball. It knocks out the fermentation gas.

li: Crush {cans} can(s) of peeled tomatoes by hand (no blender, no cooking).
Season with 4–5 g of salt per can. No sugar.
Cut {cheeseTotal} g of mozzarella into small pieces and let it drain.
Top element at {top} °C, bottom element at {bottom} °C.
If you have an infrared thermometer, measure the centre of the stone and note it down.
items.tip: warn|On the first bake (bottom ~390–410 °C) the base charred before the top was done. That's why the bottom was lowered.

li: One dough ball at a time. Dip it lightly in flour.
Press from the centre outwards with your fingertips, pushing the gas towards the rim.
Leave a 1–1.5 cm rim unpressed. On the first bake, 2 cm made the cornicione too thick.
Finish by hand to ~30–32 cm. No rolling pin.
items.tip: warn|Knock the excess flour off the base. Loose flour on the stone burns and turns bitter.

li: {sauce} g of sauce, {cheese} g of mozzarella spaced out, basil and a drizzle of olive oil.
Leave patches of tomato showing.
Before launching, give it a small sideways shake: the whole pizza must slide.
Prosciutto and rocket go on after the oven.
At 25–30 s, check whether it has enough structure to turn 180°.
Then make small turns until the colour is even.
The first pizza calibrates the oven. Use the diagnosis below.
Let the stone recover before the next pizza.
items.tip: Look for small dark spots spread across the cornicione, not black patches.

about.sub: What this site is, and where the pizza it teaches comes from.
site: NapoliProtocol is the record of a real process: the pursuit of a true Neapolitan pizza made at home, without a wood-fired oven. Every number in the recipe, every step and every rule came from bakes that were tested, logged and corrected.

Instead of a fixed recipe, the page works as a tool. You enter the flour or number of pizzas, your fridge temperature and when you want to bake, and it recalculates quantities, schedule and instructions. The tags on each step show what comes from the base recipe, what was adapted and what was learned the hard way.
Created by Jhonathan Sousa. It's an independent project with no sponsorship: the brands mentioned (flour, tomatoes, oven) are simply the ones used in testing.
pizza: Neapolitan pizza was born on the streets of Naples between the 18th and 19th centuries as cheap, popular food ready in minutes. Tradition says that in 1889 the pizzaiolo Raffaele Esposito honoured Queen Margherita with a pizza in the colours of Italy: tomato, mozzarella and basil. The Margherita was born.

What defines Neapolitan pizza is the dough: just wheat flour, water, salt and yeast, stretched by hand with no rolling pin. Baked for 60 to 90 seconds in a very hot oven, around 430–480 °C, it stays soft and elastic in the centre, with a tall, airy cornicione marked by small dark spots.

In 2010 the European Union registered it as a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed (TSG), and in 2017 UNESCO inscribed the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. At home, ovens rarely reach those temperatures, and closing that gap is exactly what this protocol is about.
